Our research provides both direct and induced representations for its simple roots, as well as determinate information about the highest weight generators that form a part of its integrable series. This analysis is then applied to a specific subset of affine Lie algebras, specifically those with nonzero central extension, to derive their associated simple root systems and highest weight generators in their irreducible representations.

The category of polar catalogs holds significance in understanding the nature of low-mass X-ray binaries that exhibit neutron star rotations. However, the majority of these sources have either unconfirmed or unreliable parallaxes, complicating conventional distance-based spectral analyses. A novel approach is presented that utilizes X-ray hardness ratios in place of spectral analysis to differentiate between asynchronous and synchronous polars. This method leverages machine learning algorithms to classify the X-ray behavior of both asynchronous and synchronous polars based on their energy spectra. Utilizing large datasets of X-ray observations, our results indicate that asynchronous polars can be distinguished from synchronous polars using X-ray hardness ratios, and that this distinction does not rely on the presence of an obvious absorption feature in the X-ray spectrum. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that utilizing this approach can yield results even when facing limited observational data for some B-band synchrotron radiation models. Building upon earlier research, our findings suggest that the polarization ratio between the ultraviolet and optical regions of the electromagnetic spectrum may be an indicator of the binary system's synchronization state, thereby providing a multiwavelegth perspective on the properties of low-mass X-ray binaries.

This study proposes a novel reduced basis method (RBM) strategy for solving
interdisciplinary problems involving fluids and structures. Initially, the
implementation employs a unified approach in which the fluid and structure
components are represented through separate reduced dimensional spaces. Subsequent
developments involve a new, integrated technique for creating a unified reduced
space across the two domains. Notably, this method can be applied to tackle
problems with disparate fluid and structure scales. Additionally, the project
investigates two methods for constructing the reduced basis functions. Furthermore,
the research introduces new technologies for solving time-dependent PDEs, including
a new, high-order discontinuous Galerkin method. These advancements are
demonstrated through simulations of a tidal blade and a cyclic vortex dynamics.

For robots to effectively navigate unfamiliar environments, having a clear understanding of their surrounding space is crucial. To this end, mapping techniques have been developed to create representations of their environment, which can facilitate efficient navigation. Although popular mapping methods provide positional information about spatial features, they lack a clear definition of spatial relationships between these features, making it difficult to build a robust navigation system. To address this limitation, our proposed HiTMap representation constructs a hierarchical diagram of spatial relationships based on feature arrangements, which can be used to navigate by predicting possible positions of features relative to others. We demonstrate the efficacy of HiTMap by comparing its navigation performance to that of a stateless navigation system in a simulated environment, showing a notable improvement in success rate with increased distance traveled.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

In atomic interferometry, typically, the local magnetic field is considered perfectly stable as any fluctuations are suppressed by intense magnetic fields. However, this study reveals that even in such controlled environments, the local magnetic field can still oscillate due to the Meissner effect in superconducting coils, exceeding 103 times that of detection sensitivity. A mathematical model has been developed to exactly describe this phenomenon and a novel method has been implemented to accurately determine the field fluctuations via atomic spectroscopy. Furthermore, this technique can be used to optimize atomic interferometry experiments in large, superconducting magnetic fields.

We investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of Janus transition metal dichalcogenides at their surface and find that they exhibit unique magnetic characteristics, with the ability to distribute charge evenly only when a specific closeness condition is met. This condition leads to the emergence of a singular energy level and allows for the efficient generation of a particular type of particle when light is applied. We demonstrate that this result leads to an unusual increase in magnetic field-induced changes in temperature and the absorption of a specific type of electromagnetic radiation. Additionally, we discover that this property allows for the efficient transmission of a specific type of particle when light is applied, leading to an increase in magnetic field-induced changes in temperature and the absorption of a specific type of electromagnetic radiation.

We investigate how electron outflow and nonlocal effects influence light behavior within a semiconductor gap, specifically in the vicinity of a quantum well. This analysis focuses on the case where the space interval between electrons and the point where the light is observed is extremely minute. Our study reveals that both electron outflow and nonlocal effects independently lead to light absorption at frequencies that would normally be reflected, and that they have a comparable magnitude. Furthermore, our findings indicate that both phenomena become more pronounced as the size of the interval decreases.

Type theory based on intuitionistic, simple types has a long-standing history, dating back to Curry's work in 1930. The addition of dependent types, introduced by Martin-L\"of in 1971, revolutionized type theory. However, the presence of defects in the type theory, such as divergent terms and inconsistent collections of types, led to the development of structured primitive proofs with normalization. This notion of normalized proofs was introduced by saleh in 1999 as the foundation for constructive mathematics. Building on saleh's framework, we introduce a novel approach called robust normalization for the calculus of constructions (CC). Our approach facilitates the expression of normalized proofs through a form of structured proofs with equality proofs, allowing us to derive key properties, including consistency, the consistency statement, and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

Our investigation focuses on the surface vortex state of a p-wave superconductor decorated with a honeycomb lattice, utilizing the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This study explores the interplay between two factors: the coupling of a lattice vibration to a specific energy level of a particle and the coupling of this energy level to a magnetic field. These interactions affect the topological properties of the system, influencing the concentration of electrons around atomic sites and the curvature of the particle's energy trajectory in response to changing magnetic field strength. Additionally, our research reveals the effect of these interactions on the system's response to a nearby reservoir that can transfer charge, and how this affects the flow of electric current induced by a small imbalance in the superconductor.

In statistics, where data varies significantly, a popular approach uses multiple components to model these variations, a technique known as finite mixture modeling. This study reveals that these models are equivalent to estimating a probability measure based on a sample, and utilizes this interpretation to recommend an alternative estimation method. Specifically, it suggests using the least squares estimator for determining the parameters of pre-specified mixture structures. Additionally, it demonstrates that the mixture models can be viewed through the lens of stochastic geometry, and employs this perspective to derive an explicit formula for bias correction in certain cases. The proposed alternative estimation method is examined under asymptotic conditions, and it shows that it competes favorably with existing methods in terms of convergence rates.

We derive the AdS$_5$-only corrections to a scalar's mass spectrum in AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ supergravity, coming from two-loop $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, for a specific set of external scalar fields. This involves calculating a specific part of the four-point amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, we find that the mass spectrum can be expressed in terms of a scale-invariant quantity related to the dual conformal field theory. This invariant is linked to the mass spectrum's specific feature, namely that certain masses remain below a certain threshold when raised to the power of $\frac{8}{(d-2)^2}$.

Concurrent memory allocation on GPUs is increasingly difficult due to their properties of fast, parallel computation, combined with separate memory and computing resources, and memory access limitations. To overcome these challenges, many applications divide memory into predetermined blocks for parallel processes, but this typically results in significant amounts of unused memory. To address this problem, we present a new, concurrent memory allocator called dynaSOAr, which is designed to meet the needs of object-based programming on GPUs. By taking a top-down approach to allocating memory, dynaSOAr is capable of creating arrays of objects with distinct sizes, and can also handle dynamic requests for memory, such as creating new objects or modifying existing ones. To improve performance, dynaSOAr is optimized for memory access patterns that are common in scientific and artificial intelligence applications, and can handle multiple concurrent requests for memory allocation. Our experiments show that dynaSOAr results in a significant reduction in memory allocation time, and improved application performance, when compared to a state-of-the-art allocator called CAO.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A new theoretical approach is presented that deviates from the traditional BCS theory and explains the behavior of superconducting-proximity phenomena through a Luttinger liquid concept. The model is specifically applied to YMn$_3$, a heavy fermion superconductor, and involves a detailed analysis of magnetic impurity states within a superconducting host. The model is then used to examine YMn$_3$ with rare earth ions replaced by Nb using a substitutional solid solution technique. Magnetic measurements and SQUID susceptibility analyses are performed on these substitutions and the results are compared to theoretical calculations to gauge the accuracy of the applied model. Additionally, the approach is also tested on a Mn-Nb(110) interface and a paired state Josephson junction formed by two Mn atoms. The findings of this research provide a clear example of how the new relativistic initial principles theory of superconductivity can be applied to explain YSR states observed in a variety of scenarios.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural architectures to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function, allowing it to adapt to various image instances. By leveraging the Fourier analysis, FourierMask can extract specific feature dimensions related to instances and ignore others. We evaluate FourierMask on the MaskRCNN benchmark and find that it significantly outperforms other dimension reduction methods while being more versatile and easy to train. Moreover, FourierMask exhibits impressive performance on the Dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple challenging datasets.

This study examines how an isometric embedding of a manifold K is related to its counterpart when K is partially covered by a region K' within a flat space K has a specific dimension and certain geometric characteristics. We demonstrate that an immersion of K that respects its geometry when restricted to K' can be mapped to an immersion of K' with particular characteristics. We also show that every immersion of K' that has these characteristics originates from an immersion of the entire domain K. This connection holds for both minimal surfaces and higher-dimensional manifolds.

The nature of highly turbulent, three-dimensional convective clouds remains elusive despite their widespread influence on the Earth's energy balance. These clouds pose a challenge in retrieving global solar cloud properties from space, as they can block most of the incoming solar radiation and obscure details of the cloud structure. This study combines high-resolution images from the MODIS and MISR to map the spatial relationship between solar radiation transmitted through these clouds and the spatial arrangement of cloud particles within them. This relationship is characterized as the "Veiled Core" phenomenon, where the lowest radiation levels are often observed at the geometric center of these clouds. By analyzing this pattern, this study reveals that the Veiled Core is a critical feature of clouds exhibiting high spatial and temporal variability within a specific latitude range. It is hypothesized that the formation of the Veiled Core is a result of a scale length associated with the size of waterfalls or shallow flows producing the cloud's upward moisture flux. A model incorporating this scale length and two key parameters from the k-epsilon turbulence model is used to simulate the transmission of solar radiation through these clouds, providing a potential framework for identifying and analyzing these clouds from space.

Our analysis takes into consideration a complex issue affecting ion thrusters, which can lead to a decline in efficiency when propelling high speed spacecraft. This performance limitation arises from the interaction between the thruster's exhaust and the surrounding spacecraft, resulting in a reduction of energy output due to thermal radiation. To overcome this challenge, we propose using a high power optical signal, which, when characterized by a specific frequency pattern, can create a 'chirp'. This 'chirp' signal, once directed at the thruster, can generate a phenomenon known as photo syndonization, which creates a 'window' of maximum energy release. As a result of this 'window', the energy output from the thruster is optimized, leading to a significant improvement in propulsion efficiency. To validate our approach, we developed a comprehensive model of the photochemical reaction, along with a new method of solving highly complex differential equations, which predicts a notable increase in propulsion efficiency, potentially exceeding 5 fold.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune candidates with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate with a short period of $4.159$ days. By calculating the potentials for these planets, researchers found that the Earth-sized candidate, named TOI-712b, has conditions suitable for life and orbits the star at a distance that could allow liquid water to exist. Analyzing the star's spectral energy distribution and using models for contraction, the team estimated the planets' masses. The results indicated that the Earth-sized candidate, TOI-712b, has a mass slightly greater than that of Earth. The team also analyzed the star's luminosity and temperature to determine the planets' distances from the star. Based on these calculations, TOI-712b was found to be the innermost planet in the system. The team is awaiting observations from ground-based telescopes to confirm the findings and gather more

This study explores the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within a rutile TiO2 structure using a semi-ab initio method. A suite of hybrid density functional theory codes was employed to examine various magnetic arrangements around the defects in order to determine their associated energies, and whether they correlated with inferred experimental findings. Our results indicate one-electron states in both carbon and nitrogen defect systems, with energy levels that could contribute to solar-spectrum energy absorption. Our data also reveal anti-ferromagnetic arrangements of electrons could increase binding energy compared to ferromagnetic arrangements, although the difference is minimal (around 0.1 eV). Our research suggests nitrogen defects have a stronger tendency to attract electrons and a greater impact on TiO2's ferromagnetic properties compared to carbon defects. Our findings support the idea that nitrogen-doped TiO2 has improved photocatalytic properties due to enhanced energy levels and magnetic arrangement, and could contribute to improved performance in solar water splitting and other photocatalytic applications.

Despite being discovered over two decades ago, top quark properties still need to be clarified, particularly its elastic scattering cross-section. This paper suggests employing vector boson production, specifically $t\bar{t}W$ and $t\bar{t}Z$ production, as a means of determining the elastic $t\bar{t}$ cross-section. It demonstrates that with 300 fb$^{-1}$ of data at the Large Hadron Collider, the elastic cross-section can be as low as 0.1 pb, thus making it feasible to establish a crucial quark property measurement.

Previous research revealed the complexity of the intra-cluster medium's structure function spectrum. Determining the nature of this complexity with observations is a priority. However, current measurements are constrained by the sensitivity of existing data and the characteristics of radiometric errors, which are not yet fully understood. To make progress, the effects of radiometric errors on structure functions needed to be characterized. By analyzing simulated observations of a numerical model with varying signal-to-noise ratios, the impact of radiometric errors on structure function estimates was investigated. The results showed that in regions with strong signals, the typical characteristics of intraday variability are retained, but with poorer accuracy. The power spectral density analysis confirms that the power spectral density is reduced by up to 5 orders of magnitude due to radiometric errors. The power lost below 10^-3 Hz is irreversibly lost due to the noise, a phenomenon that cannot be overcome with greater signal-to-noise ratios. The power spectrum of radiometric errors itself falls at around frequency of 10^-4 Hz, a critical threshold for future observations. To accurately determine how the intra-cluster medium varies, observations with a minimum sensitivity of 0.01 ks^x (where x is between 0.4 and 0.7) are required. The effects of radiometric errors need to be considered when analyzing similar observations of other astrophysical systems.

In an infinite graph $G$, a particular property is considered Ramsey for a given class of subgraphs if there exists a number $N$ such that in every 2-colored copy of some infinite pattern, either all nodes have the same color. This study focuses on finding the largest proportion of nodes with a specific color in Ramsey sets of infinite graphs, where the number of distinct colors is infinite. We achieved this by showing that in many cases, a property is Ramsey with a certain density, and that this density can be less than the highest possible density. Additionally, we established that certain properties are Ramsey with a certain density, and this density can be less than the highest possible density. This was done by using an infinite sequence of colored triangles to show that some properties have a high Ramsey density, and by using a technique called "Four Motion" to show that others have a low Ramsey density. We also found the exact density of some properties, and determined the smallest density with which a property appears in an infinite sequence of subgraphs. This research is connected to another problem related to Ramsey theory, and we made significant progress on solving it.

Located within the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation of molecular activity that is significantly aligned with the galaxy's rotational plane. By examining the mass distribution within this area, researchers can gain valuable insights into the galactic center's mass arrangement, a crucial factor in determining the spin parameter of the galaxy. A novel statistical analysis method is introduced in this study to determine the anisotropic mass arrangement in the CMZ. This method, called the second order two-dimensional correlation function, is particularly useful for identifying patterns of mass distribution that exhibit a specific orientation. By applying this method to a comprehensive dataset of molecular hydrogen observations in the CMZ, researchers discover that the mass arrangement follows a two-dimensional structure, characterized by a major axis aligned almost perpendicular to the direction of galactic rotation. Furthermore, by analyzing the mass distribution in the CMZ using a simplified radiative granular ring model, researchers find that the mass arrangement exhibits a distinct pattern that is correlated with the direction of radial motion, a feature that may be common to other ring-like structures in the galaxy.

This research focuses on detecting Bell's Palsy solely using video recordings of a person's eyes. We utilized a highly efficient, eye-centered model that only processes 2D eye movements and uses 2D eye position information from pre-trained facial features. In order to train and evaluate the model, we created a unique dataset consisting of short video segments labeled for Bell's Palsy. The results showed that the eye-centered approach led to superior accuracy compared to conventional methods using full video segments, with an impressive 92% accuracy. Notably, our method discovered distinct differences in eye behavior between people with Bell's Palsy and healthy individuals, especially in areas such as eye movement patterns and facial skin behavior.

The quantum electrodynamics in su(2) invariant space, known as sQED, is a highly promising framework for the study of quantum systems that can represent light as qubits or qutrits. Investigating the performance of qutrits, or three-level systems, in sQED, we find that their higher stability compared to qbits is crucial, with an error margin of around ten times better, as demonstrated by a quantum circuit synthesis application. Furthermore, we observe that the transition from a two-level to a three-level system significantly improves the complexity of implementing the sQED model, with an increase in gate fidelity, but at the cost of increased resource consumption in the form of entanglement. Additionally, we discover that utilizing qutrits enables more intricate quantum states, including a state with ten levels of superposition, and that the spectrum of qutrits supports more distinct sound frequencies.

The concept of generating highly polarized thick positron fluxes through laser-pulsed thin targets is based on the interaction of ultra-strong laser radiation with matter in the quantum electrodynamic limit. To overcome the limitation of requiring highly precise pulse shaping, we have theoretically and numerically analyzed the effect of illuminating thick targets with pulses that are not perfectly aligned with the water window spectrum. Our results show that even with a 100 times larger target thickness, the positron polarization remains greater than 0.1 when using a 10 fs pulse, and this to some extent can be understood by analyzing the polarization of the photon field. However, when shortening the pulse to 5 fs, the polarization of the photon field becomes insufficient, and positron polarization drops below 0.1 for any target thickness. Additionally, our findings indicate that the formation of a critical density region within the target can be avoided by using longer pulses, and this leads to a significant increase in the polarization of the positron flux. These results provide a foundation for employing thick target facilities, such as the 10 GeV linac at the University of Texas at San Antonio, to explore positron polarization in the quantum electrodynamic regime.

A set of integers is considered a limited set if the ratio of its largest size to the smallest absolute value is finite. This paper examines certain limited integer sets known as polynomial sets, which are defined as those whose values correlate with the outcomes of multiple polynomial equations following a specific pattern. The paper goes on to establish the equivalence between polynomial sets and a different class of limited sets, specifically those whose smallest and largest values have a logarithmic ratio of growth. The connection between polynomial sets and sets that fit certain geometric patterns has already been established; this paper extends that connection to any limited set with a specific pattern. The four-dimensional space of possible patterns remains unexplored in this context.

This research develops a temperature detector module with accuracy and minimal energy consumption. The device utilizes a bipolar CMOS-AI architecture and features a tiny design, incorporating two extremely sensitive parallel paths to accurately detect slight temperature variations. With no calibration required, the temperature detector demonstrates high precision, reaching an absolute error of 1.4°C. Capable of functioning effectively across a broad temperature range, this design offers extremely low energy consumption, capable of operating at as little as 0.6V, making it suitable for trendy low-power electronic systems.

The stability of magnetic fields in stars is a critical aspect in defining the longevity of stars and determining the points at which magnetic explosions, such as solar flares and giant flares, occur. This task is complicated by the need to simultaneously observe the magnetic field's strength and structure. However, recent discoveries using the Stokes V technique in spectro-polarimetry, particularly with the introduction of high-precision techniques, have facilitated detailed investigations of stars with long-axis aligned magnetic fields. This special issue provides an in-depth examination of unstable magnetic fields in stars through analytical and numerical models, as well as theoretical frameworks, and highlights the importance of further observational studies using magnetic field mapping.

Using the functional renormalization group (FRG), researchers can obtain a detailed understanding of how physical properties evolve as a parameter is varied in a quantum field theory. The FRG flow equations resemble those found in the renormalization group approach, allowing the calculation of physical observables as a function of a parameter such as temperature or the number of flavors in a theory. In this paper, we demonstrate a precise, quantitative approach to solving the flow equations, leveraging an expansion in derivatives to represent the propagation of fluctuations in terms of polynomial functions of the scale parameter. This method is highly versatile, enabling the description of renormalization group flows in quantum field theories whether they are perturbative or non-perturbative. We apply this technique to the O(N) model in zero-dimensional space, a simple model that represents multiple scalar fields interacting in a symmetric manner, in Part I of this series. Additionally, we extend the approach to a broad class of renormalization group flows, encompassing both FRG and renormalization group flows, by allowing the effect of fluctuations to be represented by a non-derivative interaction. This extension facilitates the precise calculation of physical observables in quantum field theories, whether they are zero-dimensional scalar theories or theories involving fermions and gauge fields.

Music search applications are extremely popular, yet competing systems continue to struggle in achieving high accuracy across various queries. This disparity is particularly evident when comparing the performance of music search technologies to the precision achieved by standard search engines for other forms of content. One possible explanation for this discrepancy lies in the unique structure and format of musical content. Music is composed of multiple elements, including tempo, genre, and instrumental components, which are not Composed into a single, unified whole. In contrast to other forms of content where a unified representation exists, learning multi-task learning strategies among these diverse elements appears essential for developing effective musical search techniques. With this goal in mind, a meta music search learning framework is proposed that leverages multi-task learning to combine different music elements as part of a single, integrated representation. The proposed framework is designed to be flexible and is effectively applied to two distinct music datasets utilizing a strong baseline multi-task learning model. Experimental results show that the proposed framework delivers substantially better search performance, achieving a 12% improvement in mean average precision at a recall of 0.05, or a 25% improvement when using a more stringent recall metric of 0.5.

We establish a link between geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and stacks, and a specific type of algebraic variety known as quotient varieties of algebraic groups. This connection is made clear through the use of a specialized tool from the subject. Additionally, we demonstrate how configuring objects like manifolds, algebraic varieties, and geometric spaces among others leads to a broader category that includes stacks as its fundamental building components. Furthermore, we identify key properties of these configured objects and how they relate to the underlying structure of stacks.

A massive molecular core, discovered in the Dragon infrared dark cloud, has been found to have characteristics indicative of its own dynamical evolution. The core, with a mass five times that of the Sun, is separated into two distinct parts by a thin membrane. Observations reveal the core's internal temperature is around two and a half degrees Kelvin, and its internal density is so high that it cannot support the formation of massive stars. A potential explanation is offered that the core's formation of such high-density regions may be the result of an expansion caused by its own internal gravity, leading to a shift in its density distribution. This theory may provide a model for preventing the formation of massive stars through the creation of highly dense areas, thus preventing a massive star from forming in the main plane of the galaxy.

Godel's son, Ivan Godel, developed a variant of modal logic known as S5G, which is an expansion of traditional S5 logic that includes distributivity and a binary entitlement operator. Researchers have subsequently investigate various expansions of S5G, including its relational semantics and certain equivalence theorems. This paper builds on those findings by presenting multiple new expansion sets for S5G, including its guarded version and relations with multiple accessibility links. It also proves multiple new equivalence theorems for these expanded sets and demonstrates the theorems' applicability using modified versions of epistemic scenarios.

LiDAR technology is widely used for gathering detailed information about the locations, shapes, and sizes of objects in various environments. It produces massive datasets of three-dimensional data points, which can be complex to manage and interpret. These datasets hold significant potential for training machine learning models to predict real-world outcomes, such as the risk of specific roads leading to cars being stuck in mud. However, creating a unified framework for comparing the efficacy of different learning algorithms in LiDAR datasets remains an unsolved problem. To address this challenge, researchers developed a framework for comparing point cloud datasets and associated metadata. They demonstrated the versatility of this framework by comparing several leading point cloud classifiers using six publicly available datasets from various environments. The results showed substantial variations in the performance of these classifiers, with predictions being influenced by factors such as the level of noise in the data and the method of data split. To ensure the reliability of these findings, the study included multiple random trials of all experiments. The research also highlights several outstanding research opportunities in this field, including the development of more effective techniques for handling class imbalances and noisy data, as well as the need for larger datasets spanning a wider range of scenarios.

This study extends the concept of one-step relations to spherical stochastic fields, incorporating the effects of anisotropic variation and simulation of artificially created fields. The proposed model combines the principles of Krigage and simulation, providing accurately predicted mean values and realistic patterns of variation. Formulas have been derived for estimating one-step and multi-step predictions, their variances, and the covariance between predictions and actual values. The proposed method has been demonstrated through a practical application involving the simulation of artificially created fields. The derived formulas can be applied to spherical fields in general, allowing for the simulation of fields with distinct features such as stationary, anisotropic, and non-stationary characteristics.

As neutrinos and ultra-high-energy cosmic particles aren't directly observable, their source locations can't be determined through detection alone. Based on six years of data from IceCube's neutrino academy, a statistical approach was utilized to analyze spatial connections between neutrino and UHECR arrival points. Using this method, a notable excess of UHECR spatial correlations with neutrinos was discovered for events with energies above 0.1 EeV, a phenomenon not observed in random UHECR sets. These findings suggest that many UHECR sources might be linked to neutrino sources, with the proportion increasing with UHECR energy, a relationship that needs further confirmation.

The flow resistance posed by liquid foams is significantly influenced by two main factors: the roughness of the foam's surface and the randomness of the underlying substrate. While previous research has examined the effects of surface roughness and rugosity on flow resistance, our studies reveal that surface roughness dominates the resistance experienced by a flowing liquid, outweighing the impact of rugosity. The relationship between surface roughness and flow resistance follows a specific pattern that varies with different geometric measurements, leading to various interpretations of roughness-driven resistance. Our findings are illustrated through experiments involving the flow of liquid through various types of foam layers, as well as simulations of those experiments. Additionally, our research introduces a novel category of flows characterized by intricate connections between the fluid's motion and its surrounding environment, which we refer to as 'rough bed flows.'

This study employs deep learning to identify outlier tissue samples containing carcinoma and surrounding normal tissue samples from a collection of histological images. A deep learning technique known as the disorder-aware deep network is used for this purpose. The proposed framework consists of two components: a disorder-aware deep feedforward network and a classification module. The feedforward network extracts feature vectors from histological images, while the classification module identifies normal and abnormal samples based on the extracted features. A dataset of 102,000 microscopic image patches obtained from histological images of skin carcinoma was used to train and evaluate the proposed framework. The results show that the proposed framework effectively distinguishes normal and abnormal samples, outperforming existing approaches. Furthermore, the results indicate that the proposed framework's accuracy can be enhanced through the removal of outlier samples during training.

The interplay between surface tension and rotation in a confined cell leads to an intriguing phenomenon, which creates non-standard finger patterns that adapt to various fluid levels. Typically, the Branching Hele-Shaw cell exhibits a stable finger pattern, but this stability is overthrown when the cell is inclined at a critical angle, resulting in a bifurcation and the emergence of an irregular finger pattern. This breakdown of symmetry occurs because of the presence of a poorly rotating core, which then leads to a further distortion of the fluid level and eventually produces multiple, complex finger patterns. This interaction between the rotating core and surface tension allows the finger pattern to adjust dynamically in response to changes in the level of the fluid. This adaptation is demonstrated through a series of experiments and supported by a theoretical analysis that explains the development and bifurcation of the finger pattern.

In this work, a novel approach is presented to address the constraint issue in surface phase space, centered on the unconstrained gradient method. The surface constraint is represented as an exact Hamiltonian differential equation, considered autonomous in nature. The proposed technique involves determining the entire set of Hamiltonian trajectories that pass through the surface, establishing a direct connection between the surface constraint and the Hamiltonian dynamics. The key advantage of this approach is the capability to expand the phase space volume without restriction, facilitated by the generation of additional integrals of motion, an inevitable consequence of Hamiltonian dynamics. The resulting scheme is a hybrid of molecular vibrations and rotations, emulating the behavior of independent harmonic oscillators and rigid rotors. With this method, the expansion of phase space volumes is prevented, as expected in quantum mechanics, where rotation within finite periods results in the expansion of phase space volumes, albeit in tiny increments. The proposed approach is utilized to investigate the expansion of phase space volumes in both constrained and unconstrained environments, including comparisons with existing theories.

Scientists have long analyzed the chemical composition of the TMC-1 molecular cloud to understand complex molecular formation processes. Previous studies have particularly focused on cyclopentadiene and its derivatives, revealing the presence of CCH and CN-attached ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers for the first time. By comparing their abundance, researchers found that ethynyl cyclopentadiene has approximately twice the abundance when attached to carbon in a bond, and both species show similar structure sizes as seen in their carbon-nitrogen attached counterparts. This discovery helps refine the formation process of these five-membered ring systems and highlights the significance of nitrogen-bearing molecules in forming more intricate hydrocarbons.

Our proposed approach introduces a novel interpretation of the attention mechanism in neural networks, specifically addressing the generative aspect. We contend that attention is not merely a sumptive operation, but rather one that is both predictive and focal. To illustrate this, we utilized a simple, hypothetical example. Additionally, we discovered that modeling attention within a focused space yields beneficial results, as confirmed by our experiments, which showed a notable increase in performance when incorporating this approach into baseline models.

The success of advanced computational methods in science and engineering is often hindered by the significant amount of processing power required, necessitating the development of computational paradigms that leverage multiple computers. The basis for these systems is the concept of cooperative computation between machines, and a translational approach can facilitate collaboration between programming models by creating bridges between them. We propose utilizing a language-based approach to create a common framework for programming various types of computers, and a hybrid model that combines declarative and imperative elements. This hybrid model can serve as a common language for expressing program transformations, and therefore, a unifying framework for different programming models. We applied this approach in developing a system for grid computing, specifically in a project involving ocean surface path finding, where we leveraged a combination of distributed and parallel computing to optimize performance.

A new model has been presented, based on a combined dark substance scenario, where the universe's matter and dark energy components are linked through an equation of state that reacts to the universe's expansion rate. A key feature of this model is the variation of the dark energy density in proportion to the cube of the universe's scale factor. This model is a simplified version of the Cubic Fluid Dark Energy Model, and is characterized by a constant proportionality factor that influences the dark energy density. This model exhibits a constant equation of state when the proportionality factor is set at zero. The model has been tested against observational data from supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and binary galaxy observations, and found to fit within the model's uncertainties. Furthermore, the model predicts a minimum scale factor at approximately $10^{-12}$, beyond which the universe's expansion accelerates.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a passion for living.  Unfortunately, many students lose their curiosity at a young age.  Therefore, it is essential to investigate how students develop curiosity in educational environments.  One such environment is classroom learning, where students' curiosity can be sparked by teachers' influences or classmates' interactions.  However, measuring students' curiosity in classroom learning settings is complex due to the need to consider multiple perspectives, including emotional, cognitive, and social aspects.  Additionally, learning environments involve dynamic processes that unfold over time, making it necessary to examine changes in students' curiosity levels.  Therefore, this study combines qualitative and quantitative approaches to conduct multi-method, multi-wave, and multi-perspective empirical studies of how students develop curiosity in classroom learning environments.  Specifically, it employs structural equation modeling with longitudinal data and follow-up interviews to gain a deeper understanding of the results.  Furthermore, this study introduces a novel theoretical framework that incorporates dynamic and spatial perspectives on curiosity, and utilizes structural equation modeling to examine the effects of cognitive, emotional, and social factors on curiosity levels in classroom learning environments, and explores the role of noise as both a causal and effect variable.  The findings of this study provide valuable insights for educators on how to design innovative learning activities that promote curiosity, and a practical approach to assessing curiosity levels in classroom learning environments.  Additionally, the study offers recommendations for educators on how to implement successful learning

In our research, we expand on the traditional Mat\'ern Gaussian family in a multi-dimensional space by incorporating exponential decay characteristics on a given graph. This family of functions serves as a basis for stable and efficient approximation of quasi-periodic functions. Building on the underlying Gaussian properties, we establish multiple key theorems regarding the Mat\'ern Gaussian matrix's invertibility, spectral characteristics, and the optimal recovery error for functions represented on the graph. These findings hold significant value for the development of efficient methods for recovering and interpolating functions on a range of applications, including signal processing and machine learning.

The optimal detection of areas in metropolitan cities using mobile detectors, such as self-driving cars, is a critical problem in locating hazards, managing traffic, and optimizing the delivery systems for ridesharing vehicles. This problem can be addressed by formulating a variant of the suspect target problem, where the aim is to identify areas based on ridesharing vehicles' location history and associated probability distributions. We have developed a method for solving this problem using a target identification function, which is implemented using a convolution thresholding technique. Specifically, we propose using optical character recognition and map matching to identify locations based on vehicles' license plate images, while assuming that the probability distribution of license plate images follows a gamma function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting simulations with real-world data and analyzing the impact of various parameters on the performance of our method.

Our research explores the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light scalar fields with neutrino and dark energy properties. To understand these implications, we first analyze the J/ψ decay using a Monte Carlo method and then establish a bound on the invisible decay rate. This rate is found to significantly constrain models of light scalar fields, particularly when they involve a loop containing neutrinos or photons. For example, the efficiency of these models is reduced by at least a factor of ten million due to the neutrino loop, making them challenging to validate through experiments on neutrino properties. The model's viability also depends on the relative masses of the scalar field and the J/ψ particle, with the constraint being less stringent when the scalar field is more massive. The work presents a theoretical framework that can be used to evaluate the implications of J/ψ decay into invisible matter for models of light scalar fields.

Second-order differential equation problems are typically solved using the SHSSIM method, a variable-order algorithm based on the SSIM technique. We now adapt this approach for general ODEs, establishing a variable timestep version of the new method. Key characteristics and advantages of this new algorithm are discussed in the report.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive description of the MFSSA procedure along with a demonstration of its effectiveness through a simulation study. Furthermore, we showcase the utility of MFSSA through its application to real-world data sets in economics and physiology.

In recent times, the implementation of significant economic policies has heavily relied on complex general equilibrium models, with researchers using these models to evaluate taxation, trade, and other policies. However, the accuracy of these predictions has been questioned due to significant deviations between model projections and actual outcomes. This paper delves into the limitations of these models, specifically the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models used in academia. It examines the potential for these models to produce unreliable results because of the absence of robust checks on the models' solutions, regardless of whether they are obtained through linearized approximations or more complex models. This issue becomes more pronounced in macroeconomic models that incorporate multiple sectors. The paper suggests potential safeguards for evaluating these models, such as conducting sensitivity analyses with a focus on the most vulnerable components, as well as assessing the consistency of model parameters. It also implies the need for a more critical examination of the underlying assumptions in these models.

This paper examines the time a stochastic process spends within a predetermined distance of its initial value, focusing on one-dimensional random walks with constant mean and variance. Regardless of the walk being Gaussian or not, we derive an asymptotic approximation of this time by analyzing the properties of the cumulative distribution function at zero. This connection is based on the central limit theorem, and we explore how the walk's distribution affects this relationship.

The IShTAR plasma generator, part of the STAR suite at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany, is designed to test plasma diagnostics and sampling tools for future stellarators. It produces a linear helicon plasma in a chamber with a 1.4-meter length and 0.1-meter width, operated at pressures between 0.1 and 1. Paul, and with plasma densities ranging from 1 x 10^19 to 2 x 10^19 m^-3. Due to the limited size of its chamber, plasma analysis using a global model was not feasible, so a local model was utilized instead, focusing on the plasma area near the sampling and diagnostics tools. The model was validated using experimental data collected during two experimental campaigns in 2010 and 2012, and it performed accurately in reproducing measured values of plasma density, temperature, and flow velocity. Any discrepancies found were attributed to the generation method used in the experiment, specifically the helicon source, and further improvement to the source is planned before future experiments.

The model presented in this work simulates the systemic impact of a biocontrol agent on a plant-inflicting pathogen within the plant's vascular network, incorporating competition for nutrients and limited agent distribution. A key aspect of the model identifies the critical spreading threshold for the biocontrol agent, reducing the pathogen's nutrient uptake and ultimately leading to the pathogen's extinction. This analysis provides the foundation for evaluating the efficacy of various formulations of microbial pesticides.

This study presents a novel nucleus segmentation method suited for histopathological tissue samples. Unlike traditional methods that solely rely on model predictions, our approach correctly identifies and segments nuclei by combining explicit boundary detection with implicit model predictions. We've designed a dual-stage network to achieve this combination, using one-stage to estimate nucleus masks and another to refine those estimates. Notably, our approach accounts for overlapping nuclei by incorporating implicit representations of tissue samples. We've tested this method on actual data and compared it to existing segmentation methods, demonstrating its superior performance.

We establish the converse theorem for extensions of odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups over a local non-archimedean field that are associated with a specific characteristic and high-weight parameter. Additionally, our findings include a regional version of the converse fourier transform for these groups.

A graph G is considered to have an "iterated line graph property" if applying its line graph operation repeatedly a finite number of times will eventually reveal a hamiltonian path. This paper investigates various characteristics of G's hamiltonian pathway index, including determining a lower bound for this index, establishing specific conditions for it to be equal to 2, and providing an algorithm to calculate its value exactly when G is from a particular class of graphs known as the cyclic graph.

Cell death through pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can have both beneficial and harmful effects on patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, potentially contributing to the development of severe disease manifestations. The onset of systemic pyroptosis may lead to severe inflammation, while pyroptosis in specific cells can aid in eliminating the virus. A mathematical model has been developed to describe the progression of SARS-CoV-2 within host cells, focusing on pyroptosis and the impact of anti-inflammatory treatment. The model reveals how pyroptosis can contribute to the clearance of the virus in lung cells but may cause harm in other cell types, and that timing is crucial in determining the effectiveness of anti-inflammatory treatment in controlling pyroptosis and managing the infection's clinical symptoms.

External state variables and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can compensate for insufficient internal knowledge using their knowledge of the environment. However, relying on external information may lead to overfitting and failure to generalize. This knowledge usually takes the form of external state variables and reward signals. It is observed that models trained with RL that have access to this information may perform poorly in comparison to those without it. Further, it is shown that removing this information yields better results, particularly in tasks that require generalization, than including it. Additionally, the benefits of omitting this information are found to extend across various types of RL algorithms as well as different measurement methods for evaluation. It is concluded that incorporating external information and state variables in RL typically hinders performance and impedes generalization.

A blockchain-based smart contract platform like Tezos can benefit from a validation tool like HELMHOLTZ, which uses refinement types to ensure contracts function correctly. By employing the Hindley-Milner type system and user-defined functions for type validation, HELMHOLTZ makes Tezos smart contracts more reliable and efficient. Furthermore, by drawing from refinement types, HELMHOLTZ makes these contracts more precise and able to handle properties beyond type-related issues. In addition, by using Michelson within the Haskell programming language, HELMHOLTZ provides a more user-friendly and efficient validation experience compared to other methods. This results in simpler code, better performance, and fewer errors during validation.

Graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) extend conventional convolutional neural networks to process graph-attached images by employing a fixed filter that adapts to specific objects within a fixed image region to a particular object within a particular image area. We investigated the underlying philosophy of GCNNs and discovered that their approach is analogous to the matched filtering method from signal processing. In this method, a pre-determined signal pattern is used to identify a specific signal pattern within a larger signal context. Similarly, the GCNN filter serves as a pre-determined pattern to recognize a specific object within a larger image context. Our analysis of the GCNN philosophy through the matched filtering method provides a clear and intuitive understanding of GCNNs, their strengths and limitations, and how they compare to traditional CNNs.

By modifying the Chern-Simons action in three dimensions and incorporating a scalar field, a gravity theory similar to the Einstein-Hilbert action is derived for a specific Chern-Simons partition function. This new gravity framework includes a stable spinning black hole with a "hairy" structure and a soliton, capable of representing charged particles with spin. Furthermore, this new gravity framework accurately describes solutions for spinning hairy black holes and solitons when compared to the Einstein-Hilbert action, and it also accurately describes solutions for static hairy black holes and solitons when the Chern-Simons term is ignored. The new gravity framework can also describe solutions for black holes and solitons with non-Abelian gauge fields.

The proposed concept of non-reversible symmetry is explained, along with its underlying theory. Non-reversible symmetry occurs when a reversible transformation meets specific criteria, involving an unusual parabolic matrix that sets the stage for a discussion about the Branes framework. The connection between the Branes group, obtained through hyperbolic extensions of parabolic subgroups, and the non-reversible symmetry group is explored. A simple example from the Branes dataset, specifically Branes 13, is used to illustrate the relationship between the Branes group and non-reversible symmetry. A new classification for the Branes datasets is presented, based on the non-reversible symmetry concept.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in different directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal propagation direction. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited pulse aperture results in distorted images and biased estimation of lateral shifts. To address this, a virtual origin SA (VOSA) technique is proposed, utilizing the distinctive characteristics of the modified broadband pulse to recover the under-lapping samples from the SA data. A numerical simulation and an in vitro experiment validate the VOSA approach, demonstrating the enhanced accuracy of lateral shift estimation and resulting elastographic images in comparison to the conventional SA technique.

This paper introduces an visual representation of pseudocode, incorporating graphical elements, that is designed to engage students in the study of computer science algorithms. The 'Rational Pseudocode' framework aims to bridge the gap between code and demonstrations, allowing students to explore the underlying logic of programs through interactive visualizations. By leveraging the structure of pseudocode and combining it with computational tools, this approach makes algorithms more accessible and fun for students to learn and understand. The paper outlines the design principles and educational benefits of Rational Pseudocode, providing a specific example of its application in a codeless implementation of the binary search algorithm.

We examine Boolean structures based on posets with a V-shape and determine the number of possible patterns that can be found within them, specifically focusing on V-shaped posets with three steps. This analysis enables us to derive a precise value for the Ramsey number associated with a particular pattern consisting of two distinct elements. Additionally, our work explores the number of possible patterns associated with posets with more than three steps and provides lower and upper bound estimates for these patterns. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the Ramsey number associated with a specific pattern and another related value, referred to as the character of that pattern. By establishing this connection, we are able to determine some posets' character values and others' upper bounds.

In the context of high-dimensional data, a new variant of the $k$-means clustering algorithm has been developed to address real-world challenges. The 'dynamic $k$-means' problem involves making a single pass through the data to create optimal or near-optimal $k$-means clusters without prior knowledge of $k$. Originally considered infeasible due to theoretical limitations, recent studies have achieved promising results by assuming side information about data density. Unlike previous approaches, the proposed dynamic $k$-means algorithm for high-dimensional data operates under the assumption that there are distinct regions with significant volume ratios. By applying a novel metric and a novel search algorithm, the proposed method provides a near-optimal $k$-means solution or a significant reduction in cost with only one pass through the data. Moreover, the algorithm's performance was demonstrated on real-world high-dimensional data with an order of magnitude increase in data size since the current state-of-the-art was first published.

We introduce hierarchical modes of gameplay on a grid, incorporating random elements, where players can establish sub-agreements that supersede their basic rules of interaction. The primary agreement and all secondary contracts must conform to a set of strict criteria. We explore how the potential outcomes of these complex agreements can be effectively quantified using a metric that reflects the players' individual abilities. We then examine two specific scenarios: a scenario where the grid is divided uniformly, and a scenario where the grid is divided irregularly. In the case of uniform division, we find that the optimal arrangement of gameplay is characterized by a distinct property. In the case of irregular division, we find that the optimal arrangement of gameplay is more complex and cannot be characterized by a single property alone.

A likelihood function that is circularly symmetric around a specific value $θ_0$ and varies nontransitively with the data $x$ has unique peaks at $θ_0$, thereby satisfying the fundamental requirement for a method of estimation. This characteristic applies to both parametric and nonparametric scenarios. It can be proven that a likelihood function meeting these criteria at $θ_0$ will reach its maximum value at $θ_0$ for certain alternative models as well. It is also shown that a nontransitive likelihood function can be formulated using arbitrarily small portions of the data, thereby demonstrating the versatility of this approach. Furthermore, this work is concluded by highlighting the implicit property of exchangeability among replicate observations that is inherent in the use of likelihoods.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the current implementation of this method is restricted by the fixed adapter module with fixed affinity, which is not adaptable to different image domains and limits the restoration effectiveness. To address this issue, we present a new cycleGAN framework based on an adaptive switch module, allowing both source and target domains to learn and generate interchangeable images. This module's adaptive ability prevents domain lock-in, enabling the extraction of rich and comparable feature maps that lead to more significant enhancement. We have evaluated our method against leading cycleGAN and unsupervised restoration algorithms using publicly available datasets, and the results consistently show that our approach outperforms the competition in restoring high-quality images from low-dose CT scans.

Recent successes in dialog comprehension tasks have relied heavily on pre-trained models and large-scale datasets. However, current models fall short due to their limited ability to learn from partially labeled dialog contexts. To address this, we introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model that learns from partially labeled data in a semi-supervised manner. It combines a pre-trained dialog comprehension model with a classifier using a classifier token, and extends the BART model with a self-supervised contrasting objective function. Additionally, it utilizes a tree-structured mask strategy to focus on essential elements in the dialog context. We conducted extensive experiments on the Dialog8B dataset, consisting of 257 tasks with up to 32-million partially labeled training dialog contexts. Our findings demonstrate that SPACE-2 achieves notable improvements over other baselines in a low-label setting, and is particularly effective at handling complex dialog contexts with multiple turns and roles. It also outperforms the original SPACE model, which lacks a self-supervised contrasting objective function, in all main metric categories. Moreover, our code and model parameters are available for download at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2.

This paper establishes a geometric framework within an ideal fluid spacetime that is subjected to a specific soliton development. Initially, we define a conformal Yamabe metric within the ideal fluid spacetime and demonstrate that it becomes a soliton when combined with a specific flow and vector field, resulting in the conservation of certain quantities. Notably, this relationship is expressed through a conservation law derived from the soliton development, yielding a conservative law with source and sink components that relate the soliton development to both the fluid density and the shear rate of the fluid. Additionally, we identify an integral form of this soliton development within compact regions of spacetime.

To study the distortion effect on rotating halos, we utilized the finite range simplified liquid drop model to calculate mass properties and radius parameters for $^{132}$Sn and $^{132}$Te. We found that the properties obtained with and without distortion consideration show distinct differences. Without considering distortion, $^{132}$Te's neutron separation energy and single particle level in the continuum are overestimated, while rotation properties are significantly underestimated. In contrast, using distorted potentials to describe the interactions, we achieve consistent results for energy thresholds and single particle levels in the continuum, and a notable improvement in rotation properties is observed. Furthermore, we investigated how the distortion effect influences $B_{2}(0^+ \rightarrow 2_1^+)$ probability distribution within the continuum and found that it remains robust for $^{132}$Sn but drops to a mere 0.01% with the distortion effect included for $^{132}$Te. Additional calculations for $^{132}$Ce and $^{132}$Zr yield comparable energy thresholds and single particle levels in the continuum with and without distortion consideration.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recursive application of a super-resolution filter, however this method suffers from severe flaws, especially circular reference and the tendency to over-smooth. To overcome these issues, researchers typically employ non-recursive methods, despite the inherent difficulties in video SR owing to temporal under-knowledge. Utilizing a bidirectional transformer in an extended video SR framework, our BasicVSR++ model leverages contextual information across the entire video sequence, enabling efficient direct video SR. The innovative strategy of this model, which includes temporal feature alignment and enhanced information transmission, enables each frame to learn from the optimal nearby neighbors. Through rigorous experiments, our enhanced model achieves superior performance on real and synthetic video SR datasets, outperforming the state-of-the-art in both metrics-based and video-based evaluation.

This research paper addresses a critical limitation in the current understanding of muon interactions at the TeV scale. Although next-generation muon colliders would accurately measure vector boson exchanges, it is essential to develop more precise methods for estimating the status of the detector within that environment. The paper presents an optimization technique, based on instrumental signals from peaking events, that provides accurate vector boson transfer function estimates. Tested against simulated data for various scenarios, this technique shows a level of precision that could significantly contribute to the effectiveness of future muon colliders.

In complex reinforcement learning systems, multiple components are often trained to solve a range of tasks, with shared underlying models playing a key role in the infrastructure. When changes occur during training, having a modular structure with separate domains can help prevent issues from spreading and affecting the entire system. In our research, we took a large-scale multi-task reinforcement learning platform with numerous tasks and a range of state dimensions - the MultiX environment - and designed it to incorporate modular systems. By doing so, we found that this setup significantly reduces the amount of disruption caused by overfitting, generalization issues, and other problems that arise during training. As a result, the models learn more efficiently and effectively, even when the training process is prolonged. We were able to achieve these benefits without sacrificing too much performance, as our approach only resulted in a minor reduction in the final score.

This paper provides a novel proof for the convergence of approximate gradient schemes to the solution of porous medium type and swift diffusion type equations on a noncompact metric measure space with compact boundary. The analysis relies on a new estimate for the exponential type BMO moment inequality on a noncompact metric measure space with compact boundary.

Twenty-five years before the famous meeting of Alan Turing, Emil Post, and Kleene at the 1947 Princeton conference, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was honoring the memory of three influential mathematicians and philosophers from the 19th century with a beautiful mathematical concept. This concept, involving a specific type of sentence now known as the Godel-Carnap sentence, played a significant role in Leibniz's development of the idea that the world has an objective, truth-based structure. As the field of mathematics evolved, this sentence became a key tool for addressing a broader issue related to the nature of mathematics. It enabled researchers to investigate the relationship between the concept of a universal system and the inherent properties of that system. This line of inquiry ultimately led to a deeper understanding of the fundamental characteristics of a system that is universally applicable.

This paper formulates three-sphere theorems for functions solving the complex Dirac equation, which is a key aspect of complex Clifford analysis. We establish specific conditions enabling functions to be expressed using a series expansion, similar to functions exp(ikx) and their conjugate in real analysis. These conditions are analogous to those developed by M. Ruzicka and J. Taskovic in their work on the real Dirac operator.

The extensive use of mobile devices in outdoor locations requires the daily collection of a substantial amount of spatial data, which can result in significant time and money expenditures for surveyors, engineers, and researchers. Present methods of sampling, such as systematic and random sampling, may not be suitable due to the uneven distribution of certain attributes within the area in question. This research introduces three new methods of consecutive equitable sampling, which can be used for collecting spatial data. The proposed techniques are based on sorting the region into zones based on the density of the existing points, using a distance metric that considers both Euclidean and density factors, and a method that combines the two previous approaches. An evaluation of the techniques was conducted using real-world data from weather station locations and Monte Carlo simulations, and the results showed that they outperformed the standard methods.

In our study, we offer a novel approach for educating human assistants to adjust the position of a camera attached to their hand, using a single image. This approach can be applied to assign new task frames in a robotic task that requires the camera to be positioned and oriented in a specific way relative to objects in its field of view. Our method primarily leverages a robust and flexible framework that defines object relationships and their meanings, allowing us to generate relevant training data and evaluate our training method against alternative training strategies. This method can be applied to a wide range of tasks that involve adjusting the camera to optimize its view of objects.

In various applications, researchers face the difficulty of recovering input data based on given output observations, a process known as inverse problems. Although traditional regularization techniques can effectively constrain models, they sometimes fail to capture the complexity of relationships between inputs and outputs, particularly when these relationships are multifaceted. In such cases, using a well-posed ill-posed problem formulation becomes essential. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that combines regularization and regularization-free optimization techniques to solve inverse problems through forward analysis. Specifically, we leverage a conditional generative adversarial network that incorporates two main components: a regularization-free discriminator using sampling-based adversarial training and a learned encoder as the generator. By incorporating the encoder, we can achieve reduced overfitting and improved flexibility in modeling unknown probability distributions. We also derive an iterative optimization algorithm to solve the proposed regularized conditional generative adversarial network formulation. To evaluate the performance of our method, we conduct numerical experiments in solving two inverse problems with noisy and multi-dimensional inputs, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency compared to traditional techniques.

This paper examines the absence of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems of non-integral order. By highlighting the differences between the fractional and integral cases, we demonstrate how the former is linked to the system's overall stability. We then derive a novel criterion for the absence of invariant surfaces in fractional order systems, which is expressed in terms of the system's stability at specific points. This discussion also highlights the differences between the non-integral and integral cases. To support these findings, we include numerical evidence and a brief overview of the underlying mathematics.

Next-generation wireless networks requiring ultra-high bandwidths could greatly benefit from Terahertz communication's capacity, but they're prone to distortion due to high frequency and limited physical distances available for transmission. As a result, THz devices need to form temporary, interconnected chains to enable data transmission. Nevertheless, Jakes' famous argument is less relevant here, as spatial interferences are severe in these chains, particularly in areas where uplink and downlink transmissions overlap. To address this challenge, we're investigating the application of deep reinforcement learning to optimize beam training procedures, aiming to minimize latency and improve overall performance in these scenarios.

The interstellar medium is understood to be a complex, dynamic system, though its exact dynamics remain unclear. To gain insight, researchers studied the scintillation patterns of pulsar B1133+16, which exhibited distinct features indicative of an intervening interstellar screen. By analyzing these patterns and estimating the screen's distance, velocity, and density, a detailed picture of the interstellar medium in the Galactic halo was revealed. The findings indicate the presence of dense irregularities at large scales, approximately 100 astronomical units in size, and the possibility of the interstellar medium being affected by the halo's shear layer. Further study of pulsar scintillation could provide valuable data for investigating the interstellar medium.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to input frequency parameters via dilated convolution layers with dynamic temporal resolution. Secondly, the model is optimized for quasi-periodic signal structures by stacking periodic layer modules in a cascaded manner, following the traditional quadree construction. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate superior results in both subjective listening tests and objective metrics in terms of quality and naturalness when comparing generative models with and without frequency parameters, as well as in pitch control without loss of expressiveness in limited cases.

This research presents a novel annotation platform called MADARi, which caters to the needs of standard Arabic texts. MADARi offers a range of features to support the morphological analysis and spelling correction of Arabic words within user-submitted texts. A key aspect of the platform's design revolves around the use of a modular morphological analyzer called Buhdah, which incorporates multiple analyzer engines, including Morphanity and Al-Maghraib. Unlike conventional annotation tools, MADARi incorporates a unique feature called the Spelling Adjuster's Interface, which enables users to correct the spelling of words directly from pre-trained lists, incorporating suggestions from multiple sources such as Arabicspelling and Al-Muhaddithon.
